segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Once, while the crowd was pressing in on him and listening to the word of God, he was standing beside Lake Gennesaret,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he saw two boats lying at the lake’s edge. The fishermen had got out of them and were washing their nets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He got into one of the boats, the one that was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowds from the boat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Master, we worked hard all night and caught nothing. But at your word I will let down the nets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had done this, they enclosed a great number of fish, and their nets were beginning to tear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came, and they filled both boats, so that they began to sink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at the knees of Jesus and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go away from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For amazement had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish they had taken,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were in partnership with Simon. Then Jesus said to Simon,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they had brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in one of the towns, there was a man covered with a skin disease. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am willing. Be made clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once the skin disease left him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he ordered him to tell no one:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Instead, go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing as Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the news about him spread all the more, and large crowds were gathering to listen and to be healed of their illnesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he himself would withdraw to deserted places and pray.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One day, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem; and the power of the Lord was present for him to heal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then some men came carrying on a bed a man who was paralysed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him in front of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him, stretcher and all, through the tiles into the middle, in front of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw their faith, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Friend, your sins have been forgiven you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scribes and the Pharisees began to reason,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who is this man who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, aware of their reasoning, answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you reasoning this way in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins have been forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said to the paralysed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I say to you, get up, pick up your stretcher, and go to your house.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he stood up in front of them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went off to his house, glorifying God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Astonishment seized them all, and they glorified God. They were filled with fear and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have seen extraordinary things today.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he went out and noticed a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he left everything behind, got up, and began to follow him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Levi gave a great banquet for him in his house, and there was a large crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining at table with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees and their scribes were grumbling to his disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to turning back.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John’s disciples fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Can you make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also told them a parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “No one tears a patch from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. Otherwise, he will tear the new, and the patch from the new will not match the old.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one puts young wine into old wineskins. Otherwise, the young wine will burst the skins; it will be spilled, and the skins will be ruined.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No, young wine must be put into new wineskins.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one who has drunk old wine wants young, for they say, ‘The old is good.’”

notes.note: This is the body of water that Matthew, Mark and John call the Sea of Galilee. Luke consistently calls it a lake, the more exact term for an inland body of fresh water. Gennesaret was the name of the fertile plain on its north-western shore.

Most translations have simply ‘catch’, echoing ‘fishers of people’ in Matthew and Mark. Luke’s verb is not a fishing term: it means to capture alive, and in the Septuagint it is used of sparing the lives of captives in war. ‘Alive’ is kept here because that is the element the verb specifies. Its only other New Testament use is 2 Timothy 2:26.

The Greek word, like the Hebrew term it translates in Leviticus 13–14, covered a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean. It is not the specific illness now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease), and may not have included it. Most translations keep ‘leprosy’ and explain this in a footnote. The man asks to be made ‘clean’ rather than healed because the condition barred him from normal community and worship.

Leviticus 14 requires a person whose skin disease has cleared to be examined by a priest and to bring prescribed offerings before returning to ordinary life. ‘A testimony to them’ may mean proof to the priests or to people generally that the man is clean; the Greek does not specify.

Many later manuscripts read ‘to heal them’, and the King James tradition follows that reading. The earliest witnesses have ‘him’ as the one doing the healing, which is the reading translated here. ‘The Lord’ in this phrase refers to God, whose power is at work in Jesus.

These men collected tolls and customs duties on goods, usually working for contractors who had bought the right to collect them. Some scholars prefer ‘toll collector’ for that reason. They were widely regarded as dishonest and as collaborators with Rome or its client rulers, which is why they are paired with ‘sinners’ in verse 30.

‘Repentance’ now centres on feeling sorry. In the Gospels the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

The Greek is literally ‘the sons of the bridal chamber’, a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party. It may mean the guests in general or the bridegroom’s attendants in particular, and translations vary between the two. Fasting during a wedding celebration would have been unthinkable.

Most translations have ‘new wine’ and ‘fresh’ or ‘new’ wineskins. The Greek uses two different adjectives: one meaning recent or young for the wine, and another meaning new or unused for the garment and the wineskins. ‘Young’ and ‘new’ keep the two apart. Wine that is still fermenting would split old skins that had lost their stretch.

This verse is absent from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts, though most scholars consider it original to Luke. Many later manuscripts read ‘better’ in place of ‘good’; the earliest witnesses have ‘good’. The saying is usually taken as a wry comment on those who are content with the old and will not try the new.

Frequent in the Synoptics; ‘tax collector’, ‘toll collector’ and ‘publican’ are all in use and readers would be confused by variation.
Very frequent in the Gospels and Acts; ‘scribe’ suggests a copyist, whereas the role is a trained expert in the law, and translators differ (‘scribe’, ‘legal expert’, ‘teacher of the law’).
A Luke-only form of address to Jesus (seven times) that needs to be kept distinct from κύριος, διδάσκαλος and ῥαββί consistently across the Gospel.
The contrast with νέος recurs (new covenant, new creation, new self), and one decision is needed on whether and how English distinguishes the two words.
